name: Liposomal IGF-1

lead: Liposomal IGF-1 is a topical idea for thicker scalp hair: deliver the growth factor IGF-1 to hair follicles inside fat-like carriers.

IGF-1 is made naturally by follicle cells, and a 2025 review reports that it stimulates follicle proliferation and blood vessel growth and extends the growth phase through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signalling. The supporting work is laboratory and animal research; no human hair-loss trial of a topical liposomal form was found.

paras: It is discussed in hair-loss communities as a scalp product applied topically, often next to established hair treatments. Hair changes are generally judged over several months.
Safety of topical IGF-1 on the scalp has not been established in published trials. It is an unapproved product for hair.

web.title: IGF-1 in Hair Regeneration (PMC full text)

angle.text: Liposomal IGF-1 is meant to carry IGF-1 to the follicle, extend the growth phase and give thicker scalp hair. In lab work IGF-1 promotes follicle proliferation; human trials of the topical form have not been found.

lead: Liposomal IGF-1 is insulin-like growth factor 1 packaged in liposomes, tiny fat-based carriers, for application to the scalp. The aim is to deliver a growth signal to the hair follicle so that follicles stay longer in the growth phase, which in turn could support thicker, denser-looking hair. [1]

IGF-1 is a 70-amino-acid hormone made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone. [2] In hair, it is made mainly by dermal papilla cells at the base of the follicle; a 2025 review describes it as acting through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signalling to promote follicle proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, extend the anagen (growth) phase and raise VEGF, which supports blood supply to the follicle. [1][3] The same review reports that IGF-1 and VEGF are lower in dermal papilla cells in androgenetic alopecia. [3]

The liposomal gel format has been tested in animals: a 2012 hamster study by Castro and colleagues used 1% and 3% liposomal IGF-1 gels and reported thicker, faster-growing hair in the 3% group without a rise in plasma IGF-1 or liver enzymes, as relayed on the HairLossTalk forum. [3][4] Reviewers note that most evidence is preclinical and that topical IGF-1 has a short half-life and low skin permeability. [3]
infobox: Hair follicle dermal papilla, IGF-1 receptor [3]
Not an approved hair treatment; mecasermin is an injectable IGF-1 analogue approved for severe IGF-1 deficiency in children [2]

paras: Dermal papilla cells mainly secrete IGF-1, which binds IGF-1 receptor and activates PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways that promote follicular cell proliferation, inhibit apoptosis and push follicles into the anagen phase. [3] IGF-1 raises VEGF expression, supporting angiogenesis and nutrient delivery, and appears to dampen TGF-beta1, a known inhibitor of hair growth. [3] The review links lower IGF-1 and VEGF in androgenetic alopecia to androgens such as DHT. [3]

Because IGF-1 has a short half-life and low skin permeability, topical IGF-1 has been tested mainly as liposomal gels, which showed improved penetration and hair density or thickness in animal and some human reports. [3] Proposed improvements include fusion proteins with Fc, albumin or transferrin and plant-derived exosomes. [3]

The 2025 review says topical IGF-1 showed no systemic toxicity in animals and did not raise circulating IGF-1; clinical safety evidence it cites comes mainly from hearing-loss trials rather than hair studies. [3] Systemic IGF-1 therapy for growth hormone insensitivity has caused transient effects such as hypoglycemia and facial coarsening, with a few benign and malignant tumours reported as treatment-emergent events but too few for risk estimates. [3] Wikipedia notes that high IGF-1 levels are associated with cancer in observational data, while both high and low levels raise mortality risk. [2] Several authors of the review disclose ties to Schweitzer Biotech Company. [3]

Topical IGF-1 has been tested outside hair: a randomized trial in the middle ear used IGF-1-impregnated gelatin hydrogels for sudden deafness refractory to corticosteroids. [5][6] That work concerns hearing rather than hair.

No studies found of a liposomal IGF-1 scalp product in a published human trial. The 2025 review summarises mouse, hamster and rabbit studies and cultured human follicle experiments, including 1994 work in which IGF-1 elongated cultured human follicles in a dose-dependent way, [3] and mentions limited clinical data. A registered 2026 trial compares a scalp elixir with 5% minoxidil in 40 people with hair loss, though it does not specify IGF-1. [7]
